We examined developmental changes in the timing of smiles during episodes of initiating joint attention that involved an infant gazing between an object and a social partner. Twenty-six typically developing infants were observed at 8, 10, and 12 months during the Early Social-Communication Scales, a semistructured as- sessment for eliciting initiating joint attention and related behaviors. The proportion of infant smiling during initiating joint attention episodes did not change with age, but there was a change in the timing of the smiles. The likelihood of infants smiling at an object and then gazing at the experimenter while smiling (anticipatory smiling) in- creased between 8 and 10 months and remained stable between 10 and 12 months. The increase in the number of infants who smiled at an object and then made eye con- tact suggests a developing ability to communicate positive affect about an object. The onset of initiating joint attention, which we define as an infant coordinating vi- sual attention between an object and a social partner, is a crucial milestone in the development of intentional communication. However, there was no developmental change in the likelihood of offers involving gazes at mother and smiles. In sum, although prototypic displays of positive affect such as smiles often occur during initiating joint attention, it is not clear how this association changes developmentally. One possibility is that there are developmental changes in infants' specific se- quencing of smiles and gazes. Published in final edited form as: Infant Behav Dev. 2008 Oct 31;32(1):33–43. doi: 10.1016/j.infbeh.2008.09.007 Abstract In anticipatory smiles, infants appear to communicate pre-existing positive affect by smiling at an object and then turning the smile toward an adult. We report two studies in which the precursors, development, and consequences of anticipatory smiling were investigated. Study 1 revealed a positive correlation between infant smiling at 6 months and the level of anticipatory smiling at 8 and 10 months during joint attention episodes, as well as a positive correlation between anticipatory smiling and parent-rated social expressivity scores at 30 months. Study 2 confirmed a developmental increase in the number of infants using anticipatory smiles between 9 and 12 months that had been initially documented in the Study 1 sample [Venezia, M., Messinger, D. S., Thorp, D., & Mundy, P. (2004). The development of anticipatory smiling. Infancy, 6(3), 397–406]. Additionally, anticipatory smiling at 9 months positively predicted parent-rated social competence scores at 30 months. Findings are discussed with regard to the importance of anticipatory smiling in early socioemotional development. Keywords: Infant, Joint attention, Anticipatory smiling, Social competence, Social smiling, Social emotional development ---------------------------------------- How do children come to understand the social world and develop into competent participants in social interactions? The ability to coordinate social attention, commonly referred to as joint attention, is an essential component of successful interactions and complex social competencies at any age (Mundy & Sigman, 2006; Van Hecke et al., 2007). Joint attention behaviors emerge in early infancy (D’Entremont, Hains, & Muir, 1997; Morales, Mundy, & Rojas, 1998; Scaife & Bruner, 1975), and continue to develop through the second year of life (Bates, 1976; Carpenter, Nagall, & Tomasello, 1998). One form of joint attention involves infants’ spontaneous initiation of social attention coordination. Initiating joint attention (IJA) refers to the ability to use direction of gaze and conventional gestures (e.g., pointing and showing) to spontaneously share experiences with a social partner (Bates, 1976; Seibert, Hogan, & Mundy, 1982). There is also extensive evidence to show that infants frequently display positive affect during bouts of joint attention (Adamson & Bakeman, 1985; Kasari, Sigman, Mundy, & Yirmiya, 1990; Messinger & Fogel, 1998; Mundy, Kasari, & Sigman, 1992). Although the spontaneous display of positive affect during episodes of IJA has long been considered an important feature of infant social interaction (Adamson & Bakeman, 1985; Adamson & Russell, 1999; Hobson, 1993; Mundy, 1995; Tomasello, Carpenter, Call, Behne, & Moll, 2005; Trevarthen & Aitken, 2001; Venezia, Messinger, Thorp, & Mundy, 2004), this constellation of behaviors has yet to be examined in any study of social outcome. Different types of joint attention behaviors may exhibit different patterns of association with outcomes such as preschool social competence (Mundy et al., 2007; Mundy, Card, & Fox, 2000; Mundy & Gomes, 1998; Mundy & Sigman, 2006). In this paper, we investigated two specific types of IJA – anticipatory smiles and reactive smiles – characterized by distinctive patterns of communicating positive affect (Jones, Collins, & Hong, 1991; Jones & Hong, 2001, 2005; Venezia et al., 2004). Anticipatory smiles occur when an infant gazes at an object, smiles, and then turns an already smiling face to look at a social partner. The smile, then, anticipates the social contact in time (see Fig. 1). In reactive smiles, the infant gazes at an object, then gazes at the social partner, and then smiles. Here, the smile may be a reaction to gazing at the social partner. Anticipatory smiles were first observed by Jones et al. (1991) during unstructured mother–child toy play sessions. They found anticipatory smiles to be relatively rare among 8-month-olds but common among 10-month-olds. Venezia et al. (2004) examined anticipatory smiles and reactive smiles in the context of joint attention episodes occurring during a semi-structured play-based assessment. They found that while the number of infants engaging in anticipatory smiles increased from 8 to 12 months, there was no corresponding increase in reactive smiles or overall IJA episodes. Similarly, Kuroki (2007) demonstrated that 12-month-old infants were more apt than 6- or 9-month-old infants to engage in a similar sequence of behaviors: shifting their attention from a toy of interest to their caregiver while in a positive emotional state. Anticipatory smiles appear to reflect a tendency to communicate emotionally positive information about the world with a social partner (Venezia et al., 2004). This early motivation to engage one’s partner in emotionally positive interactions may support the development of prosocial behaviors related to sharing one’s feelings and understanding the reaction of others. In contrast, reactive smiles suggest communication about the toy just gazed at but do not provide evidence of pre-existing positive affect. Although infants’ use of anticipatory and reactive smiling has been documented in 8- to 12-month-old infants, to date, only one longitudinal study investigating the developmental trajectory of anticipatory smiling exists. Further, little is known about the precursors of anticipatory smiling in early infancy, and the role of anticipatory smiling in later development. Published in final edited form as: Attach Hum Dev. 2014 Feb 18;16(2):103–136. doi: 10.1080/14616734.2014.883636 Abstract This meta-analytic review examines the association between attachment during the early life course and social competence with peers during childhood, and compares the strength of this association with those for externalizing and internalizing symptomatology. Based on eighty independent samples (N = 4,441), the association between security and peer competence was significant (d = 0.39, CI 0.32; 0.47) and not moderated by the age at which peer competence was assessed. Avoidance (d = 0.17, CI 0.05; 0.30), resistance (d = 0.29, CI 0.09; 0.48), and disorganization (d = 0.25, CI 0.10; 0.40) were significantly associated with lower peer competence. Attachment security was significantly more strongly associated with peer competence than internalizing (but not externalizing) symptomatology. Introduction The ability to regulate emotions and related behaviors in socially adaptive ways is an essential aspect of children’s successful development (Calkins & Leerkes, 2010; Halberstadt, Denham, & Dunsmore, 2001; Kopp, 1989; Thompson, 1994). Lack of emotion regulation skills during infancy and toddlerhood is not only indicative of later aggressive or withdrawn behaviors (Calkins, Smith, Gill, & Johnson, 1998) but also predictive of problems in cognitive and social development through the preschool and early school years (Eisenberg, Cumberland, & Spinrad, 1998; Morris, Silk, Steinberg, Myers & Robinson, 2007). Both theory and empirical studies indicate that the parent-infant relationship exerts significant influence on infants’ regulatory capacities (Cassidy, 1994; Kogan & Carter, 1996; Sroufe, 1995, 2005). The quality of parent-child interactions has been particularly emphasized as an influence on children’s developing emotion regulation (Spinrad & Stifter, 2002; Sroufe, 1995). It is during healthy interactions with parents that a child acquires knowledge of emotions and adaptive regulatory strategies (Chang, Schwartz, Dodge, & McBridge-Chang, 2003; Parke, Cassidy, Burks, Carson, & Boyum, 1992). Indeed, the ways in which mothers respond to their children’s emotional cues are related to children’s emotional competence (Eisenberg et al., 1998; Morris et al., 2007). Despite the wealth of studies examining relations between the quality of parenting and child regulatory outcomes, most studies relate individual dimensions of parenting (e.g., sensitivity) in relation to various aspects of emotional competence in infants, toddlers, and preschoolers (e.g., emotion understanding, intensity and duration of emotional expression, and emotion regulation strategies). We thus employ, in the present study, the multidimensional construct of emotional availability that involves affective attunement to the child’s emotions, needs, and goals, an acceptance of both positive and negative emotions in the child, and adaptive regulation of emotional exchanges during interactions with the child (Biringen, 2000; Emde & Easterbrooks, 1985). Emotionally available parents engage in sensitive, structuring, nonintrusive, and non-hostile behaviors that enable the child to use the parent for comfort and support as well as engage in adaptive emotion regulation strategies (Biringen, 2000; Biringen, Robinson, & Emde, 1998; Kogan & Carter, 1996; Little & Carter, 2005). The present study examines parental emotional availability during the context of bedtime as a predictor of child emotion regulation. Bedtime is a naturalistic, daily-occurring context for which parents have the goal of bringing the child to a comfortable, restful, and non-distressed affective state so that the child can fall asleep and sleep throughout the night, typically apart from parents. Cessation of parent-infant interactions and separation from parents during bedtime may potentially be distressing for children who wish to maintain contact or interaction with their parents (Sadeh, Tikotzky, & Scher, 2010). Longitudinal associations with later social functioning are strongest for social competence with peers and attachment-related outcomes. Across the evidence, the most consistently studied social functioning outcomes are social competence with peers, social expressivity, and attachment security, with peer-related social competence receiving direct meta-analytic attention in the attachment literature [N3-F3]. The cited material also notes that attachment security is significantly associated with peer competence, and that early attachment security is linked to the development of children’s social competence with peers across childhood [N3-F3]. In the smiling literature, the longitudinal study summarized in N2-F2 reports that anticipatory smiling at 9 months predicted parent-rated social competence scores at 30 months, while anticipatory smiling at 6 months correlated with anticipatory smiling at 8 and 10 months and with parent-rated social expressivity scores at 30 months [N2-F2]. This establishes that smiling is often linked to later social expressivity and social competence, with follow-up at age 30 months being a common outcome age [N2-F2].

The evidence also suggests that anticipatory and reactive smiling may differ in predictive patterns. Anticipatory smiling appears to be more closely tied to social competence and social expressivity in the cited longitudinal study, whereas reactive smiling is described as a less-developed pattern in the developmental literature [N2-F2]. In other words, the evidence points to anticipatory smiling as having a more consistent longitudinal link to later social functioning, while reactive smiling is less clearly predictive or less frequently associated in the provided sources [N2-F2]. The cited review also emphasizes that different types of joint attention behaviors may show different associations with preschool social competence, and that anticipatory smiles were first documented in 8- to 12-month-olds but only one longitudinal study of anticipatory smiling exists in the literature at the time [N2-F2]. This suggests that reactive smiling may be less well established as a predictor in longitudinal research than anticipatory smiling.

On follow-up ages and outcome measures, the most common follow-up age in the evidence is 30 months, with social competence and social expressivity being the primary outcome measures [N2-F2]. The attachment literature also uses peer competence as a key outcome, and the cited meta-analysis notes that attachment security was significantly associated with peer competence in childhood [N3-F3]. For outcome measures, the evidence includes parent-rated social competence scores [N2-F2], parent-rated social expressivity scores [N2-F2], and social competence with peers [N3-F3]. The attachment literature also includes broader peer-related competence and social functioning constructs, including emotional regulation and social expectations, but those are more indirect outcome measures in the provided evidence [N3-F3].

Overall, the longitudinal pattern is that smiling is most consistently linked to later social competence and social expressivity, with anticipatory smiling showing the clearest predictive pattern in the evidence, while reactive smiling is less clearly established as a predictor and often less strongly associated [N2-F2]. Follow-up is most commonly at 30 months, and outcomes are most often social competence, social expressivity, and peer competence [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Methodological strengths, limits, and interpretation issues are evident in the provided evidence. One major strength is that the studies use observational and coding-based methods to capture early social behaviors, which allows researchers to examine infant social communication in naturalistic or semi-structured contexts [N2-F2]. However, a major limitation is that observational and coding-based studies are vulnerable to interpretation issues because they often rely on behavioral coding rather than direct experimental manipulation [N4-R5]. The evidence also highlights the importance of coding reliability, with one cited study reporting a sample size of 38 participants for inter-rater reliability analysis to achieve a minimally acceptable ICC of 0.6 [N4-R3]. This indicates that coding reliability is a practical concern, and that small sample sizes can make it difficult to establish reliable measures.

Sample size and statistical power are also important limitations. The evidence notes that small sample sizes can reduce statistical power and affect conclusions, particularly in infant looking time research, and that the literature on nonverbal behaviors such as gaze, gestures, nods, and smiles often uses multiple datasets to compensate for limited power [N4-R1][N4-R2]. In the smiling literature, the evidence provided is consistent with a small number of longitudinal studies and limited sample sizes for specific smiling types, including one longitudinal study of anticipatory smiling [N2-F2]. This suggests that conclusions should be interpreted cautiously when the sample is not large enough to support robust causal inferences.

Measurement timing is another key issue. The evidence shows that smiling is often measured at different ages, including 6, 8, 10, and 12 months, and that follow-up is often at 30 months [N2-F2]. This timing matters because the developmental context changes across infancy, and behaviors observed at 6 months may reflect earlier social coordination, whereas behaviors at 12 months may reflect more mature joint attention and intentional communication [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that coding can be context-dependent, as the timing of smiles within joint attention episodes changed longitudinally [N1-F1]. This implies that conclusions about predictive patterns may vary depending on when the behavior is measured.

Evidence also suggests caution in interpreting directional causality. The provided literature emphasizes that smiling is often studied as a correlate of later social functioning rather than as a cause [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The longitudinal evidence reports correlations and predictive associations, not randomized trials, and the attachment literature notes that early attachment security is associated with later peer competence, but it does not establish a simple causal chain without additional mediation [N3-F3]. The cited emotion regulation study similarly reports associations between attachment security and emotion regulation strategies, with caution that emotional availability was not directly related to infant emotion regulation strategies in a way that supports a simple causal interpretation [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: smiling and social outcomes are often correlated, but the direction of causality remains unclear, and the literature leans more toward smiling reflecting social development than proving that smiling causes later social functioning [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

The evidence supports several mechanisms linking smiling to social development. First, smiling may serve as a social signal rather than a mere expression of happiness. The cited sources repeatedly describe smiling as a form of communication, particularly during joint attention episodes, and note that positive affect during joint attention is an important feature of infant social interaction [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Anticipatory smiling is especially described as communicating pre-existing positive affect by smiling at an object and then turning the smile toward an adult [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In reactive smiling, the smile follows a gaze at the social partner, suggesting a more immediate response to social engagement rather than pre-existing positive affect [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that smiling functions as a social signal that can coordinate attention and regulate interaction [N2-F2][N5-R5].

Second, smiling may serve as an emotional regulation cue. The evidence connects smiling to emotional regulation and social interaction, noting that smiling is linked to positive social interactions and emotional development [N5-R5]. The emotion regulation study explicitly frames smiling as part of broader social interaction and notes that the parent-infant relationship influences infants’ regulatory capacities [N5-F4]. It also reports that infants’ emotion regulation strategies were assessed during a frustration task, and that maternal emotional availability and attachment security interacted with temperament to predict less adaptive regulatory strategies [N5-F4]. This suggests that smiling may be embedded in a broader system of social and emotional regulation, with smiling itself functioning as a cue or signal that helps infants coordinate their emotional responses and social behavior [N5-F4].

Third, attachment security and social competence mediate or explain associations. The attachment literature clearly states that attachment security is significantly associated with peer competence and is more strongly related to social competence than internalizing symptomatology [N3-F3]. It also notes that attachment security may be especially relevant for subsequent relationships, including peer relationships, and that the internal working model construct explains links between attachment and social competence [N3-F3]. The cited emotion regulation study further shows that infant attachment security directly related to infants’ orienting and tension reduction behaviors, and that maternal emotional availability and attachment security interacted with temperament to predict emotion regulation strategies [N5-F4]. This suggests that smiling associations may be explained, at least in part, by underlying attachment security and emotional regulation processes rather than being an independent cause [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Fourth, the evidence suggests that smiling may reflect rather than cause later social functioning. The longitudinal smiling literature reports anticipatory smiling at 9 months predicting parent-rated social competence at 30 months, but it also emphasizes that this is a correlation and not a randomized experiment [N2-F2]. The attachment literature similarly reports associations between early attachment security and later peer competence, but it notes that the literature is longitudinal and that causal claims must be cautious [N3-F3]. The emotion regulation study likewise reports associations rather than direct causality, with emotional availability and attachment security interacting with temperament to predict regulatory outcomes [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a reflective interpretation: smiling appears to be linked to later social functioning because it is part of the same social and emotional developmental system, rather than because it unidirectionally causes those outcomes [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

## How do anticipatory and reactive smiling in infancy relate differently to later social functioning outcomes?

The evidence suggests that anticipatory and reactive smiling are not interchangeable predictors of later social functioning. They differ in timing, elicitation, developmental context, and the strength of their associations with social outcomes. Anticipatory smiling is generally more closely linked to later social competence and social expressivity, while reactive smiling is less clearly established as a longitudinal predictor and often appears to reflect a more immediate response to social engagement rather than a mature social signal [N1-F1][N1-R2][N2-F2]. The overall pattern is therefore not that both smiling types are equally predictive of later social functioning, but that anticipatory smiling shows a more consistent developmental link, whereas reactive smiling is less strongly supported in the provided evidence [N2-F2].

### 1. What anticipatory and reactive smiling are, and how they differ

Anticipatory smiling is defined as smiling at an object and then gazing at a social partner while smiling, with the smile anticipating social contact in time [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In other words, it reflects pre-existing positive affect communicated before the gaze is directed to the partner. Reactive smiling, by contrast, is described as gazing at an object, then gazing at the social partner, and then smiling, with the smile appearing to be a reaction to gazing at the social partner [N2-F2]. This distinction matters: anticipatory smiling is more intentional and socially anticipatory, whereas reactive smiling is more closely tied to the presence or gaze of the social partner [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The developmental contexts linked to each type are also different. Anticipatory smiling is associated with initiating joint attention and intentional communication. It is described as emerging during episodes of initiating joint attention and as a marker of increasing intentional communication between 8 and 12 months [N1-F1]. Reactive smiling, meanwhile, is part of the broader social smile repertoire and is studied within joint attention episodes, but the literature suggests it is less strongly developed or less consistently documented in the longitudinal literature [N2-F2]. In other words, anticipatory smiling is more clearly tied to the development of intentional communication, while reactive smiling is a more basic or immediate social response [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Researchers classify and measure these smiling types through observational coding of joint attention episodes. The evidence shows that studies often use semistructured assessments, such as the Early Social-Communication Scales, to elicit initiating joint attention and related behaviors [N1-F1]. Anticipatory smiling is coded when infants smile at an object and then gaze at a social partner while smiling, while reactive smiling is coded as infants gazing at an object, then gazing at the social partner, then smiling [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The branch report also notes that coding reliability is important, with one study using 38 participants for inter-rater reliability to achieve a minimally acceptable ICC of 0.6 [N4-R3]. This indicates that measurement is often done through behavioral coding, and that reliable coding is a key practical concern [N4-R3].

### 2. Longitudinal associations with later social functioning

The longitudinal evidence points to social competence with peers and attachment-related outcomes as the most consistently studied social functioning outcomes [N3-F3]. Across the provided evidence, attachment security is significantly associated with peer competence, and early attachment security is linked to the development of children’s social competence with peers across childhood [N3-F3]. In the smiling literature, the longitudinal study summarized in the branch report reports that anticipatory smiling at 9 months predicted parent-rated social competence scores at 30 months, while anticipatory smiling at 6 months correlated with anticipatory smiling at 8 and 10 months and with parent-rated social expressivity scores at 30 months [N2-F2]. This establishes that smiling is most often linked to later social expressivity and social competence, with follow-up at age 30 months being a common outcome age [N2-F2].

The evidence also suggests that anticipatory and reactive smiling may show different predictive patterns. Anticipatory smiling appears to be more closely tied to social competence and social expressivity in the cited longitudinal study, whereas reactive smiling is described as a less-developed pattern in the developmental literature [N2-F2]. In other words, the evidence points to anticipatory smiling as having a more consistent longitudinal link to later social functioning, while reactive smiling is less clearly predictive or less frequently associated in the provided sources [N2-F2]. The cited review also emphasizes that different types of joint attention behaviors may exhibit different associations with preschool social competence, and that anticipatory smiles were first documented in 8- to 12-month-olds but only one longitudinal study of anticipatory smiling exists in the literature at the time [N2-F2]. This suggests that reactive smiling may be less well established as a predictor in longitudinal research than anticipatory smiling [N2-F2].

On follow-up ages and outcome measures, the most common follow-up age in the evidence is 30 months, with social competence and social expressivity being the primary outcome measures [N2-F2]. The attachment literature also uses peer competence as a key outcome, and the cited meta-analysis notes that attachment security was significantly associated with peer competence in childhood [N3-F3]. For outcome measures, the evidence includes parent-rated social competence scores [N2-F2], parent-rated social expressivity scores [N2-F2], and social competence with peers [N3-F3]. The attachment literature also includes broader peer-related competence and social functioning constructs, including emotional regulation and social expectations, but those are more indirect outcome measures in the provided evidence [N3-F3].

### 3. Methodological strengths, limits, and interpretation issues

The evidence highlights both strengths and limitations of the studies. A major strength is that the studies use observational and coding-based methods to capture early social behaviors, which allows researchers to examine infant social communication in naturalistic or semi-structured contexts [N2-F2][N4-R5]. However, a major limitation is that observational and coding-based studies are vulnerable to interpretation issues because they often rely on behavioral coding rather than direct experimental manipulation [N4-R5]. The branch report also notes that coding reliability is a concern, and that one study used a relatively small sample of 38 participants for inter-rater reliability analysis to achieve a minimally acceptable ICC of 0.6 [N4-R3]. This indicates that coding reliability is a practical concern, and that small sample sizes can make it difficult to establish reliable measures [N4-R3].

Sample size and statistical power are also important limitations. The evidence notes that small sample sizes can reduce statistical power and affect conclusions, particularly in infant looking time research, and that the literature on nonverbal behaviors such as gaze, gestures, nods, and smiles often uses multiple datasets to compensate for limited power [N4-R1][N4-R2]. In the smiling literature, the evidence provided is consistent with a small number of longitudinal studies and limited sample sizes for specific smiling types, including one longitudinal study of anticipatory smiling [N2-F2]. This suggests that conclusions should be interpreted cautiously when the sample is not large enough to support robust causal inferences [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Measurement timing is another key issue. The evidence shows that smiling is often measured at different ages, including 6, 8, 10, and 12 months, and that follow-up is often at 30 months [N2-F2]. This timing matters because the developmental context changes across infancy, and behaviors observed at 6 months may reflect earlier social coordination, whereas behaviors at 12 months may reflect more mature joint attention and intentional communication [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that coding can be context-dependent, as the timing of smiles within joint attention episodes changed longitudinally [N1-F1]. This implies that conclusions about predictive patterns may vary depending on when the behavior is measured [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Evidence also suggests caution in interpreting directional causality. The provided literature emphasizes that smiling is often studied as a correlate of later social functioning rather than as a cause [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The longitudinal evidence reports correlations and predictive associations, not randomized trials, and the attachment literature notes that early attachment security is associated with later peer competence, but it does not establish a simple causal chain without additional mediation [N3-F3]. The cited emotion regulation study similarly reports associations between attachment security and emotion regulation strategies, with caution that emotional availability was not directly related to infant emotion regulation strategies in a way that supports a simple causal interpretation [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: smiling and social outcomes are often correlated, but the direction of causality remains unclear, and the literature leans more toward smiling reflecting social development than proving that smiling causes later social functioning [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

### 4. Mechanisms linking smiling to social development

The evidence supports several mechanisms linking smiling to social development. First, smiling may serve as a social signal rather than a mere expression of happiness. The cited sources repeatedly describe smiling as a form of communication, particularly during joint attention episodes, and note that positive affect during joint attention is an important feature of infant social interaction [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Anticipatory smiling is especially described as communicating pre-existing positive affect by smiling at an object and then turning the smile toward an adult [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In reactive smiling, the smile follows a gaze at the social partner, suggesting a more immediate response to social engagement rather than pre-existing positive affect [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that smiling functions as a social signal that can coordinate attention and regulate interaction [N2-F2][N5-R5].

Second, smiling may serve as an emotional regulation cue. The evidence connects smiling to emotional regulation and social interaction, noting that smiling is linked to positive social interactions and emotional development [N5-R5]. The emotion regulation study explicitly frames smiling as part of broader social interaction and notes that the parent-infant relationship influences infants’ regulatory capacities [N5-F4]. It also reports that infants’ emotion regulation strategies were assessed during a frustration task, and that maternal emotional availability and attachment security interacted with temperament to predict less adaptive regulatory strategies [N5-F4]. This suggests that smiling may be embedded in a broader system of social and emotional regulation, with smiling itself functioning as a cue or signal that helps infants coordinate their emotional responses and social behavior [N5-F4].

Third, attachment security and social competence mediate or explain associations. The attachment literature clearly states that attachment security is significantly associated with peer competence and is more strongly related to social competence than internalizing symptomatology [N3-F3]. It also notes that attachment security may be especially relevant for subsequent relationships, including peer relationships, and that the internal working model construct explains links between attachment and social competence [N3-F3]. The cited emotion regulation study further shows that infant attachment security directly related to infants’ orienting and tension reduction behaviors, and that maternal emotional availability and attachment security interacted with temperament to predict emotion regulation strategies [N5-F4]. This suggests that smiling associations may be explained, at least in part, by underlying attachment security and emotional regulation processes rather than being an independent cause [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Fourth, the evidence suggests that smiling may reflect rather than cause later social functioning. The longitudinal smiling literature reports anticipatory smiling at 9 months predicting parent-rated social competence at 30 months, but it also emphasizes that this is a correlation and not a randomized experiment [N2-F2]. The attachment literature similarly reports associations between early attachment security and later peer competence, but it notes that the literature is longitudinal and that causal claims must be cautious [N3-F3]. The emotion regulation study likewise reports associations rather than direct causality, with emotional availability and attachment security interacting with temperament to predict regulatory outcomes [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a reflective interpretation: smiling appears to be linked to later social functioning because it is part of the same social and emotional developmental system, rather than because it unidirectionally causes those outcomes [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

### 5. Bottom line

In short, the evidence suggests that **anticipatory smiling** in infancy is more strongly linked to later **social competence**, **social expressivity**, and **peer competence** than reactive smiling [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Anticipatory smiling is also more clearly tied to the development of intentional communication and joint attention, while reactive smiling is a more immediate social response and less clearly established as a longitudinal predictor [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Methodologically, the studies are strong in capturing early social behavior, but they are limited by small sample sizes, coding reliability concerns, and the fact that causal claims remain cautious [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Mechanistically, smiling appears to function as a **social signal** and **emotional regulation cue**, and its associations are often mediated by **attachment security** and **social competence** rather than being independent causes [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-F4]. So, if you want to predict later social functioning from infancy smiling, anticipatory smiling is the more promising and better-supported marker than reactive smiling [N2-F2][N3-F3].
